The brief facts that have emerged from the DAR are that on 03.07.2024, on receipt of information of an accident vide DD No.3A the information of present accident was received by the IO/ASI Virender Singh.
Thereafter, he along with Ct. Vikas went to the spot where they came to know that two injured were taken to the hospital by some public person.

IO interrogated the driver of the offending vehicle and arrested him.

19. In the present matter, the factum of the accident is not in dispute.
It is an admitted fact that the accident occurred with the offending vehicle.
It is also a matter of record that the respondent no.1 was chargesheeted by the IO.
Now, the respondents have alleged that the accident was caused due to the the rash and negligent act of the deceased.
However, no evidence was led by the respondents to prove this fact.
The CCTV footage has not been placed on record by the IO.
Same was also produced by the respondents.
None of the respondents entered into the witness box to prove the negligence of the injured persons.

The pillion rider i.e. the injured was examined as Aanam vs Jatin Khanagwal on 5 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27627003/
5 PW1 but the CCTV footage was not played to him for his cross examination also.
Hence, in the opinion of this Tribunal, the respondents have failed to prove that the accident was caused due to the the rash and negligent driving of the deceased Mohd. Farman.

20. It is pertinent to mention here that in the proceedings before the claims tribunal, the facts are to be established on the basis of preponderance of probabilities and not by the strict rules of evidence or the higher standard of beyond reasonable doubt as required in criminal cases.
The burden of proof in the present cases is much lower than as placed in civil or criminal cases.

In Bimla Devi &
Ors. v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors (2009) 13 SC 530, it has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that negligence must be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view RUCHIKA SINGLA SINGLA Date:

In the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar &
Ors. (2011) 1 SCC 34, Hon'ble Supreme Court held as under:
"General principles relating to compensation in injury cases 4.

Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar &
Ors. (2011) 1 SCC 34
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The provision of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (`Act' for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The Court or tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability RUCHIKA SINGLA SINGLA 2025.12.05 16:21:19 +0530 to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

(See C. K.
Subramonia Iyer vs. T. Kunhikuttan Nair - AIR 1970 SC 376, R. D. Hattangadi Vs.
Pest Control (India) Ltd. - 1995 (1) SCC 551 and Baker vs. Willoughby - 1970 AC 467).
5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following :
Pecuniary damages (Special Damages)

(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising :
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General Damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii)(a) and (iv)."

In view of the above law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in injury cases, award needs to be passed only under heads of medical expenses, loss of earning during treatment period and damages for pain, suffering and trauma.
However, the petitioner gave a statement before the Tribunal on 29.11.2025 that he may be awarded a fixed compensation of Rs. 2.5 lacs under Section 164 Motor Vehicle Act.

Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act is reproduced as under:
"Payment of compensation in case of death or grievous hurt, etc.

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or instrument having the force of law, the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be.

(2) In any claim for compensation under sub-section (1), the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person.

20. It is pertinent to mention here that in the proceedings before the claims tribunal, the facts are to be established on the basis of preponderance of probabilities and not by the strict rules of evidence or the higher standard of beyond reasonable doubt as required in criminal cases.
The burden of proof in the present cases is much lower than as placed in civil or criminal cases.
In Bimla Devi &
